'''''Verbena urticifolia''''', known as '''nettle-leaved vervain'''<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007|access-date=2014-10-17}}</ref> or '''white vervain''', is a [[herbaceous plant|herbaceous]] [[plant]] in the vervain family ([[Verbenaceae]]). It belongs to the "true" vervains of [[genus]] ''[[Verbena]]''.

[[File:Verbena urticifolia ÖBG 2012-05-28 03.jpg|thumb|The ''[[Urtica]]''-like leaves were the reason for the scientific name ''urticifolia''.]]

==Description==
White vervain has opposite, simple [[leaf|leaves]] on thin, rigid, green stems. The serrated leaves look similar to those of ''[[Urtica]]'', which is the reason for the plant being named ''urticifolia''. The small flowers are borne in [[Raceme|spikes]]; they open in summer and unusually for this normally bluish-flowered genus are white. The fruit is a dark-colored capsule with many brown and thin seeds. The entire plant except for the flowers and fruit is covered in stiff bristles.

==Range==
White vervain is native to eastern [[North America]], excluding [[Mexico]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.wildflower.org/plants/result.php?id_plant=VEUR |website=Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center |publisher=The University of Texas at Austin |title=''Verbena urticifolia'' |date=20 December 2019 |access-date=14 July 2022}}</ref>

==Habitat==
White vervain is commonly found growing individually in [[Ecological succession#Secondary succession|disturbed areas]] with partial shade.  It prefers [[mesic habitat]]s.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.illinoiswildflowers.info/savanna/plants/wh_vervain.htm |last=Hilty |first=John |website=Illinois Wildflowers |title=White Vervain |date=2020 |access-date=14 July 2022}}</ref>

==Relation to other vervains==
This species may be closest to a group that might include such North American species as ''[[Verbena lasiostachys|V. lasiostachys]]'' or ''[[Verbena menthifolia|V. menthifolia]]'', and the [[common vervain]] (''V. officinalis'') from [[Europe]]. Like these, it is [[diploid]] with a total of 14 [[chromosome]]s. The relationship of the [[swamp verbena]] (''V. hastata'') to these other species is more enigmatic; its [[evolution]] might have involved [[hybrid (biology)|hybrid]]ization with the white vervain or a related species in the past.<ref name = "y+o2008">Yuan & Olmstead (2008)</ref>
